It was a sunny Wednesday morning; what would normally be just another ordinary day in the middle of a workweek. But on this day, everyone stopped. Housewives abandoned their kitchens, vendors left their stalls, and butchers, storekeepers, and tailors locked up their shops—all to join the procession winding through the Jewish Quarter.

earlier, the Maharal had been chosen as the successor. And so now, as the new rav of the city, he led this crowd.

Shmuel, devoted grandson, was there to help his grandfather down the carriage steps. The Maharal was now well into his eighties; his beard was an almost transparent white, and, at times, he needed someone to support his bent frame. Once the Maharal was standing on the ground, the noisy crowd quieted.

Today, on the shloshim, we are placing a matzeiva on his grave; one that is truly fitting for a man of his stature.”

Slowly, laboriously, six burly men lifted an elaborately carved headstone off of the wagon and lowered it down onto a patch of fresh earth.

ceremony was over. The Maharal and Shmuel went back into the carriage. They had a stop to make before heading home: the Maharal was to attend a council meeting in the rauthaus.

While his grandfather went inside, Shmuel pulled out a volume of mishnayos to learn. He was still in the year of aveilus for his own father, Rav Betzalel, who had passed away right around the time of the Maharal’s appointment. It was his father’s death which had prompted Shmuel to move his family back to Prague; with his father gone, it was too painful to remain in Kellin.

Shmuel got through three mishnayos before there was a tap on his shoulder.

Shmuel looked up. It was Reb Efraim Meyers*, the interim leader of the city council.

Shmuel followed the man inside the meeting hall. The council members sat in a semicircle in the center of the room. There were nine men there, and a tenth empty chair in the center. The Maharal sat on a red-carpeted stage reserved for the chief rabbi.

Reb Efraim smiled, grabbed one of Reb Shmuel’s hands, and gave it a hearty shake. “Mazal tov, Reb Shmuel! You are to be the next Rosh Hakahal of Prague.”

‘Yes, you! Your hardworking nature, kind heart, and business sense will be of great service to the community.”
